decisions.reason: They govern different handshake messages: the server Certificate message versus CertificateVerify. Omitting one does not implement the check for omitting the other.
One constrains the client's key-establishment offer in ClientHello, while the other constrains the server's selected indication in ServerHello.
They map different HandshakeType members to different numeric values: client_hello to 1 and finished to 20.
They map different NamedGroup members to different code points: x25519 to 0x001D and x448 to 0x001E.
The identical numeric bound applies to different fields: Extension.extension_data and CertificateEntry.extensions.
They map different HandshakeType members to different numeric values: server_hello to 2 and encrypted_extensions to 8.
Both require a sent HelloRetryRequest to contain supported_versions. The canonical evidence is the direct primary-body requirement specific to HelloRetryRequest.
An unrecognized extension type and an unrecognized key share value are different inputs at different parsing scopes; ignoring one does not test ignoring the other.
One omits the server's Certificate when server certificate authentication is unused; the other requires the client's Certificate after a client-authentication request.
The same key class is described for different message sets in Figure 1 and Figure 4, so their applicability and trace checks are not equivalent.
They map different ExtensionType members to different values: server_name to 0 and RESERVED to 46.
One applies handshake traffic keys to braced full-handshake messages in Figure 1; the other applies application traffic keys to bracketed messages in Figure 4.
They map different ExtensionType members to different values: server_name to 0 and padding to 21.
One defines fallback version negotiation whenever supported_versions is absent; the other defines a protocol_version abort only for the narrower no-supported-version branch.
The Figure 3 rule is limited to a subsequent PSK handshake, while the NEGOTIATED state rule applies to the server flight more generally.
They constrain different fields and lower bounds: Extension.extension_data permits zero octets, while DistinguishedName requires at least one.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: certificate_verify to 15 and certificate_status_RESERVED to 22.

Both require the uniform bad_record_mac alert for every record decryption or deprotection failure. The canonical is the direct primary-body alert definition rather than the security-considerations restatement.
They map different ContentType members to different values: invalid to 0 and application_data to 23.
Handshake integrity and key confirmation are separate security properties and require different implementation checks.
They apply to opposite sending directions and different write IVs: client/client_write_iv versus server/server_write_iv; the second also specifies XOR construction.
They map different reserved SignatureScheme members to different values: dsa_sha384_RESERVED to 0x0502 and dsa_sha512_RESERVED to 0x0602.
They apply to opposite sending directions and different write IVs: server/server_write_iv versus client/client_write_iv; the second also specifies XOR construction.
The conditions select different key-establishment modes and require different ServerHello extensions: key_share for (EC)DHE and pre_shared_key for PSK.
They require supported_versions in different messages sent by different endpoints: ClientHello and HelloRetryRequest.
They map different SignatureScheme members to different values: rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 to 0x0804 and rsa_pss_pss_sha384 to 0x080a.
These are complementary branches, not the same check: send a client Certificate when requested versus forbid it when no CertificateRequest was sent.
One checks only Certificate-before-CertificateVerify ordering; the other additionally constrains Finished ordering and is scoped to the initial Figure 3 client flight.
They map different SignatureScheme members to different values: ecdsa_secp384r1_sha384 to 0x0503 and ecdsa_secp521r1_sha512 to 0x0603.
They map different AlertDescription members to different values: decryption_failed_RESERVED to 21 and decrypt_error to 51.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: client_hello to 1 and encrypted_extensions to 8.
EarlyDataIndication has message-dependent bodies: uint32 max_early_data_size in NewSessionTicket and Empty in ClientHello.
Both map SignatureScheme.ecdsa_sha1 to 0x0203. The canonical requirement cites the direct primary-body enum definition rather than the appendix repetition.
They map different SignatureScheme members to different values: rsa_pss_rsae_sha384 to 0x0805 and rsa_pss_pss_sha256 to 0x0809.
They constrain extension vectors in different messages and with different lower bounds: EncryptedExtensions permits zero octets, while ClientHello requires at least eight.
They constrain different extensions and allowed message sets: early_data in CH/EE/NST and signature_algorithms_cert in CH/CR.
They map different SignatureScheme members to different values: rsa_pss_rsae_sha256 to 0x0804 and rsa_pss_pss_sha512 to 0x080b.
They derive different secrets for different purposes with different labels: binder_key using ext/res binder versus the Handshake Secret salt using derived.
One requires a client Certificate for requested client authentication; the other requires a server Certificate for certificate-based server authentication.
One is the sender's ClientHello encoding rule; the other is the server's receiver-side validation rule with a mandatory illegal_parameter failure outcome.
They map different NamedGroup members to different code points: x448 to 0x001E and x25519 to 0x001D.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: certificate_verify to 15 and certificate_url_RESERVED to 21.
They constrain different extensions and allowed message sets: signed_certificate_timestamp in CH/CR/CT and pre_shared_key in CH/SH.
They map different ContentType members to different values: handshake to 22 and application_data to 23.
They constrain different extensions and allowed message sets: early_data in CH/EE/NST and oid_filters only in CR.
The key switch applies to different endpoints and states: the client after receiving server Finished versus the server after sending ServerHello.
They constrain different nested fields and lower bounds: X.509 cert_data is 1..2^24-1, while the enclosing certificate_list is 0..2^24-1.
They constrain different extensions and allowed messages: max_fragment_length in CH/EE and psk_key_exchange_modes only in CH.
One covers every TLS protocol error and allows an optional alert; the other is specifically the connection outcome for record decryption errors.
Both require TLSPlaintext.length to equal the encoded byte count of the immediately following fragment. The canonical evidence states that field relationship explicitly in the primary body.
They map different HandshakeType members to different values: certificate to 11 and finished to 20.
The Figure 3 rule also orders Certificate before CertificateVerify and applies whenever those optional messages are present; the state rule is conditioned on a requested certificate the client has.
One forbids a server Certificate when server certificate authentication is unused; the other forbids a client Certificate when no CertificateRequest was sent.
They preserve different PSK-associated parameters for 0-RTT: the negotiated ALPN protocol versus the symmetric cipher suite.
They cover opposite extension-presence branches: forbidding legacy_version negotiation when supported_versions is present versus defining fallback negotiation when it is absent.
One governs encoding every variable-length vector's actual length; the other governs the special decoding semantics of a zero length as an empty vector.
They map different SignatureScheme members to different values: rsa_pss_rsae_sha512 to 0x0806 and rsa_pss_pss_sha256 to 0x0809.
One is the client's placement obligation; the other is the server's validation obligation with a required illegal_parameter alert on violation.
The identical numeric bound applies to different message fields: KeyShareClientHello.client_shares and EncryptedExtensions.extensions.
They are different endpoint state transitions triggered by different messages: client WAIT_CERT on Certificate versus server WAIT_CV on CertificateVerify.
Although both terminate with unexpected_message, the invalid message, endpoint applicability, and protocol state differ: client receipt of EndOfEarlyData versus premature KeyUpdate.
They constrain different extensions and allowed message sets: max_fragment_length in CH/EE and certificate_authorities in CH/CR.
The server's early-data check requires exact cipher-suite equality; the client's PSK check requires Hash compatibility and has an illegal_parameter outcome.
They constrain different extension vectors with different bounds: ServerHello.extensions is 6..2^16-1, while NewSessionTicket.extensions is 0..2^16-2.
One governs whether the server sends CertificateRequest; the other governs the client's Certificate response after such a request.
